lesson_title: Collecting, Summarising and Comparing Data: Order, Count, Quarters
hook_text: Two clinics. Same country. One box plot shows a 25-minute gap in every patient's morning — and most people can't read it.
clip_script: Eleven patients at a rural clinic, seated in order of how long they waited: 20 minutes at one end, two full hours at the other. No formulas — just count. The patient dead centre of the bench? 60 minutes. That's the median, the typical visit. Cut the left half in the middle: 30 minutes — a quarter of the patients are seen that fast. Cut the right half: 90 minutes — and here's the sentence that wins exams — a QUARTER of these patients wait 90 minutes or more, every ordinary day. Now the city clinic, same country, same week: typical wait 35 minutes, longest just 55. Put both box plots on one scale and unequal access stops being a headline and becomes a picture — the rural box stretched wide, the urban box tight and short. One more secret: the average says 63,6, the median says 60. Why the gap? One patient with a lost file drags the mean; the median doesn't move for anyone. That's why house prices and salaries always quote medians — the mean can be hijacked by a single millionaire. Order. Count. Quarters. That's data handling.
visual_style: Patients seated along a clinic bench ordered by waiting time, chalk lines cutting the bench into quarters; two box-and-whisker plots stacking onto one shared scale, the rural box stretching wide in red while the urban box stays compact; the mean sliding as one outlier sits down.
mood: Sharp-eyed and socially aware, the voice of someone who reads the numbers behind the news.
pacing: Steady counting along the bench, quickening into the two-clinic comparison, a pointed slow-down on the quarter-of-patients reveal and the mean-versus-median twist.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read any graph the news throws at you.
